extracted.intended_audience: researchers and readers interested in research integrity, preprints, and mathematics (arXiv users, mathematicians, science-watchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing or assessing a news/item about an arXiv preprint withdrawal (why a preprint was withdrawn, how arXiv handles withdrawals, and the implications for readers and researchers).

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv withdrawal policy
rubrics_metrics.description: “arXiv allows authors to withdraw papers whenever they’d like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may withdraw submissions at any time; arXiv gives authors control over withdrawal timing. The page notes this as a liberal, author-driven policy without describing formal constraints or mandatory disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of explanation for a withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may provide “as much or little detail about their reasons as they care to provide.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no requirement on the level of explanatory detail; examples include a brief comment from Shoikhet: “The paper has been withdrawn due to a crucial mistake in the arguments.” News coverage may note whether the author responds to requests for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional equivalence to journal retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: “An arXiv withdrawal serves the same function as a journal retraction,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although withdrawals perform the same corrective function as retractions in journals, procedural differences exist (see visibility of prior versions). Reporters and evaluators should treat withdrawals as substantive corrections to the literature even if the mechanism differs from formal journal retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of withdrawn/earlier versions
rubrics_metrics.description: “all prior versions remain online, without notation that the paper was withdrawn. The earlier versions of Shoikhet’s post have no marks to show that it was eventually withdrawn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because earlier versions remain accessible and may lack a clear withdrawn label, readers and bibliometric systems can still access and cite potentially-superseded content. This raises transparency and discoverability concerns when evaluating the state of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use and interpretation of preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: arXiv is “meant to serve as a pre-print platform to disseminate and gain feedback on works that have not been published.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints are preliminary and not peer-reviewed; consumers should not treat preprints as equivalent to peer-reviewed publications. As a commenter put it: “If anyone uses a pre-print to draw conclusions in the same light as a peer-review paper, it should be on them.” This is both a normative and practical criterion for evaluating reliance on preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of self-correction
rubrics_metrics.description: When you find a mistake, no matter how long later, “you fix it or retract the result.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal after discovering an error is presented as consistent with scientific and mathematical norms of self-correction. The piece frames author-initiated withdrawal upon discovery of a crucial mistake as exemplary behavior rather than blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint-to-journal publication rate as a metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers have found that about “two-thirds of biomedical preprints” are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals, and the “proportion is roughly similar for preprints in physics and math.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statistic can be used as a baseline metric when assessing the lifecycle likelihood that a preprint will be peer-reviewed and formally published; deviations from these rates may be noteworthy in reporting or meta-research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between causes of retraction (error vs fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions can result from honest mistakes or from misconduct; example given: a decades-old paper retracted due to fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators and reporters should distinguish between withdrawals/retractions prompted by honest error and those prompted by fraud, since implications for the author’s conduct and for downstream reliance differ. Historical examples (including fraud) illustrate that retraction reasons affect interpretation of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: explain the nature of the mistake to inform others
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urge the author to “comment on the nature of the mistake so that others who may have relied on your paper for their own work become fully informed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not mandated by arXiv, providing a clear explanation of the error helps downstream researchers assess impact and is recommended as a community-responsible practice.
